steps.label: Conclusion (unlikely = opinion)
steps.body: It's unlikely that nanobes are living things.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: Nanobes are probably inanimate artifacts of the microscopic structure of the clay in which they're found.

steps.label: Evidence (because)
steps.body: Nanobes are 1/10 the size of the smallest known bacteria. They are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, which is a prerequisite for life.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The whole argument rests on a rule and a fact. Rule: anything alive has a reproductive mechanism. Fact: a single nanobe is too small to contain one. Put them together and nanobes can't be alive, so the geologist must be looking at bits of clay.

Given that a single nanobe is too small to hold a reproductive mechanism, how could we still argue that nanobes are living things? We can't deny the rule; it's a premise. So look at what the author assumed about how the rule applies. The author assumes the mechanism has to fit inside one nanobe. What if nanobes don't reproduce one at a time? If several could team up, the group could have the mechanism that no single nanobe can hold.

A second route goes after the author's alternative: anything that makes "inanimate artifacts of the clay's microscopic structure" a poor explanation. That one is harder to predict, so expect the first route.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that a living thing can reproduce without each individual containing the whole mechanism, for example by joining up with others. Less likely: an answer that makes the clay-artifact explanation hard to believe.

notes.body: A is about sexual reproduction in bacteria. The argument never said life requires sexual reproduction, only some reproductive mechanism, and bacteria reproduce in other ways. A says nothing about whether something one-tenth the size of a bacterium can reproduce, so the size problem is untouched.

The evidence only works if each nanobe has to carry its own reproductive mechanism. B breaks that assumption: "Single-celled creatures can combine to form a multicelled structure and then reproduce." Apply that to nanobes. One nanobe may be too small, but a group could reproduce together, so being tiny no longer rules out life.

The move to repeat: when you can't deny a premise, ask what the author assumed about how it applies, then find the answer that breaks the assumption. Here it was one individual, one mechanism.

C gives us material phenomena about the size of nanobes, but only says some scientists "claim" they are fossilized bacteria. Something nanobe-sized that we knew was alive would weaken badly. A disputed fossil isn't that, and it doesn't show anything that small ever had a reproductive mechanism.

D attacks old definitions of life built with "inferior microscopes no longer in use." The argument relies on one requirement, a reproductive mechanism, and D never says that requirement is wrong. The old definitions may have demanded the same thing. Nothing here helps a nanobe reproduce.

E says some animals are larger but simpler than others, so size and complexity don't line up perfectly. It runs the wrong way for us: we need something tiny that is still complex enough to reproduce, not something big and simple. And one fact about lizards says nothing about the scale of nanobes.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (unlikely = opinion)
old_steps.body: It's unlikely that nanobes are living things.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
old_steps.body: Nanobes are probably inanimate artifacts of the microscopic structure of the clay in which they're found.

old_steps.label: Evidence (because)
old_steps.body: Nanobes are 1/10 the size of the smallest known bacteria. They are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, which is a prerequisite for life.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This feels like a tough one to figure out on our own (we'll need the answers to help), but we can frame the right tension in our brain. Given that .. living things all have a reproductive mechanism, but nanobes are too small to have a reproductive mechanism, How could we still argue that ... nanobes are living things?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Let's look for something that helps us say, even though "nanobes are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism" it still could be the case that "nanobes are living things", after all .. [answer choice]. Or, less likely, look for something that hurts the plausibility that nanobes are just inanimate artifacts of the clay's microscopic structure.

old_notes.body: Whether known bacteria engage in sexual reproduction is irrelevant to whether nanobes are alive. Nanobes aren't bacteria. If this answer were meant to imply that bacteria isn't complicated enough to reproduce, then it would probably strengthen the argument. We know, in reality, that bacteria is a form of life (there are other forms of reproduction besides sexual reproduction, such as asexual reproduction). But if we thought this answer was saying that bacteria isn't even complex enough to be life, then that would support the author's notion that nanobes, 1/10 the size, are also not life.

I'd never dream up this answer on my own, but it gives us a way us, as the anti-conclusion lawyer, to respond to the author's evidence. US: nanobes are living things! AUTHOR: no. they're too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, which is required to be alive. US: yes, they're too small for any one individual to have a reproductive mechanism, but they can combine with other nanobes in order to reproduce. So they do have a reproductive mechanism.

If we were told about something as small as a nanobe that WAS a form of life, then that would badly weaken. These remains of bacteria are as small as a nanobe, but we're not told they're alive. They are "material phenomena". They might just be a fragment of a bacterium. The bacterium is a form of life, but the fragmented remains aren't necessarily life.

We aren't talking about previous definitions of life. The author is yielding the current definition of life, one that includes as a prerequisite that an entity has a reproductive mechanism. And for all we know the previous definition of life ALSO held that any form of life must have a reproductive method.

This is saying you can be bigger but simpler than some other animal. Being bigger doesn't necessarily mean you're more complicated. Being smaller doesn't necessarily mean you're less complicated. Could we stretch this to say, "Being smaller than bacteria doesn't necessarily mean that nanobes are less complicated than bacteria"? No, that's a big stretch. This is just one example about some cold-blooded lizards, not a rule of life we can extrapolate to the microscopic scale. At the scale of lizards and other animals near their size, everyone is WAY big enough to have DNA, a reproductive mechanism. We're talking about a thing that is INCREDIBLY small, potentially smaller than DNA itself.

steps.label: Conclusion (thus)
steps.body: Children are put at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (Evidently)
steps.body: Most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on students' posture.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In a study, all the keyboards and most monitors were placed higher than recommended for children, leading children to sit in ways that encourage craned necks, awkward wrists, and other unhealthy postures.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument makes two jumps, so there are two places to push.

Jump one: the computers are set too high, so they were installed "without consideration of their effect on posture." Given that all the keyboards and most monitors sit too high for children, how could someone still have considered posture? Maybe the computers are shared with adults and the height is a compromise. Possible, but a stretch.

Jump two is weaker. Given that children sit in unhealthy postures, how could they still not face "the same risk" as office workers? "Same" is a strong word. It assumes a child's body takes the same damage from bad posture that an adult's does, and that the exposure is comparable. Office workers sit at keyboards all day; children at school probably don't. And a child's body may handle strain differently. Either difference breaks "the same risk."

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that makes children different from office workers in a way that matters for repetitive stress injuries: less time at the computer, or bodies that handle the strain better. A less likely route: a good reason the computers were set high even though posture was considered.

notes.body: A says the recommended height differs for children and adults. The researcher already relied on that: the computers were "higher than recommended for children." A just explains why they count as too high, so it fits the evidence instead of challenging the jump to the same risk as office workers.

B is about time at home, but the conclusion is about the risk school computers create. More home use doesn't make the school postures any less harmful, and home setups could be just as bad. The impact is unclear, so B can't seriously weaken.

The researcher moves from bad posture straight to the same risk as office workers. That only works if a child's body reacts to strain the way an adult's does. C denies it: children's "greater suppleness" makes them "less susceptible than adults" to these injuries. Same postures, lower risk, so "the same risk" fails.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion says two groups are equal, look for a relevant difference between them.

D says office workers' equipment is usually at the wrong height too. That makes the two groups look more alike, which helps the comparison. To weaken, we need a difference between children and office workers, and D supplies a similarity.

E is about who reports injuries, not who gets them. Children might report fewer injuries simply because they don't recognize them or don't tell anyone. Reporting rates don't show their actual risk is lower, and the conclusion is about risk.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (thus)
old_steps.body: Children are put at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (Evidently)
old_steps.body: Most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on students' posture.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: In a study, all the keyboards and most monitors were placed higher than recommended for children, leading children to sit in ways that encourage craned necks, awkward wrists, and other unhealthy postures.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The argument makes two conclusions, so we should scrutinize each of those reasoning moves. Given that ... all the keyboards and most monitors were installed in positions higher than what's recommended for kids (giving them bad postures while using the computers), How can we argue ... most elementary school computers are installed with consideration of their effect on posture? We'd have to make up some story for why someone would consider the effect on kids' posture of installing the computers that high but do it anyway. Maybe they hate kids. Maybe they don't want kids to have too much screen time, so they want using a computer to be slightly uncomfortable. Maybe adults also need to use these computers at times, so the computers were installed in a position that tries to balance the needs of both body types. Given that ... most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on posture, How can we argue ... this does not put children at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers? We would want to make it seem like the situation with kids is different from the situation with office workers. Presumably, kids don't use the computer for as much time as adults do, so can we really say they're at the "same risk"?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an Alternate Explanation for why computers are installed in a non-kid-friendly way, an answer that makes it seem like the computer-installers do consider kids' posture, or an answer that makes it seem like the situation with kids in computer labs is not fair to equate with office workers getting repetitive stress injuries.

old_notes.body: This answer says the recommended height for computers differs between children and adults. But the argument already established that the computers are positioned too high for children — confirming that the standard is different and that the school computers do not meet the child-appropriate standard. If anything, acknowledging that children have different ergonomic requirements supports the claim that the current setup is problematic for them. This answer reinforces the premise that the computers are improperly positioned for children rather than undermining the conclusion about injury risk.

This answer says children spend more time on computers at home than at school. While this is interesting, its impact on the argument is uncertain. It could mean children accumulate more total exposure to bad posture, which might strengthen the risk claim. Or it could be irrelevant if home computers are better positioned. The argument specifically concerns school computers and their posture effects. Whether children face additional risks at home does not address whether school computer posture problems produce the same injury risk as office workers face. The argument's comparison is between school children and office workers, not between total child computer exposure and adult exposure.

This answer directly attacks the argument's bridge assumption — that similar posture problems produce similar injury risks in children and adults. By establishing that children's bodies are more supple and therefore less susceptible to repetitive stress injuries, this answer drives a wedge between "same bad posture" and "same injury risk." The argument assumed that because children experience the same types of unhealthy postures as office workers, they face the same risk of RSI. But if children's greater physical suppleness acts as a protective factor, the same postures could produce significantly lower injury risk. The posture problems are real, but the risk comparison to office workers fails because children's bodies are biologically more resilient to the specific type of damage that RSI represents.

This answer says office workers' computers are also not at recommended heights. If anything, this strengthens the parallel between children and office workers — both groups face improperly positioned equipment. The argument claims children face the same RSI risk as office workers. Showing that office workers also use poorly positioned computers supports the comparison by confirming that both populations experience similar ergonomic failures. To weaken the argument, we need a reason why the same posture problems do not produce the same risk, not additional evidence that the posture problems are comparable.

This answer says office workers are more likely to report injuries than children. But the argument's conclusion is about actual risk — the likelihood of developing RSI — not about reporting rates. Even if children underreport injuries, that does not change whether they actually face the same physiological risk. The argument is making a claim about biological susceptibility based on posture analysis, not about injury statistics based on self-reporting. Differences in reporting behavior might affect how we measure injuries, but the argument's conclusion is about whether the risk exists, not about whether it is documented.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The health risks of GMO foods are minimal.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: A GMO food can't have effects that would be significant enough to be worrisome.

steps.label: Evidence (since)
steps.body: In most cases of deliberate alteration of a plant's genes, only a single gene in 750,000 has been changed. This change is very slight.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
There are two moves here, and we can push on either.

Move one, in the last sentence: the change is slight, so it "cannot have effects significant enough to be worrisome." Does that follow? Pull the wrong block from a Jenga tower and the whole thing comes down. What matters is not how much changed but what the changed part does. If a single gene controls something important, changing it could matter a lot.

Move two: "In most cases" only one gene in about 750,000 is changed, so the risk is minimal. Most cases aren't all cases. What if the foods people worry about are the ones where many genes were changed?

Move one is the bigger target. "Cannot" is a claim about every slight change, so a single counterexample hurts it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that changing a single gene can have a significant, worrying effect. Less likely: an answer showing that engineered foods often involve more than a slight change, or direct evidence that their health risks are serious.

notes.body: A says engineered plants offer few advantages over ordinary ones. That's about benefits, and the scientist's conclusion is only about risk. A plant can be pointless and perfectly safe. A gives no reason to think a one-gene change can do harm.

B says whatever risks exist "may be somewhat reduced by other factors" such as added vitamins and minerals. That makes the risk smaller, if anything, which fits the claim that "the risk is minimal." A weakener needs the risk to be bigger than the scientist thinks.

C says scientists haven't located the genes behind every trait. That is uncertainty, and it cuts both ways: the changed gene might matter or might not. It never shows a one-gene change can have a significant effect. D gives a known case; C only gives a gap in knowledge.

The scientist's key move is that a change this slight "cannot have effects significant enough to be worrisome." D gives a counterexample: plants whose toxicity "is known to be affected by the alteration of a single gene." D speaks of toxicity to "some animals," not specifically to humans, but that is still enough to break "cannot": one gene changed, and something as serious as toxicity changed with it. The size of a change doesn't decide its effect; what the gene does decides it.

The move to repeat: when an argument says something is too small to matter, look for a case where something that small mattered a lot.

E attacks the opponents: the consumers most opposed tend to be ill-informed. Even if the critics are wrong about everything, the scientist's own reasoning could still be bad. Undercutting the other side does nothing to the step from a slight change to no worrying effect.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: The health risks of GMO foods are minimal.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
old_steps.body: A GMO food can't have effects that would be significant enough to be worrisome.

old_steps.label: Evidence (since)
old_steps.body: In most cases of deliberate alteration of a plant's genes, only a single gene in 750,000 has been changed. This change is very slight.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: There are two conclusions here, so we could potentially resist either one. The mini-argument in the last sentence is making a move from "since the change is slight, the effect wouldn't be significant". Does that have to be true? Can slight changes have significant effects? I know sometimes I only pull our one Jenga tile but the whole tower comes crashing down. So one way to weaken would be to present information suggesting that slight changes can have significant and possibly worrisome effects. The other move is that "Since most case of deliberately altering a gene involve only a slight change (that couldn't produce a significant effect), the risk of GMO foods is minimal." Does that have to be true? How do we know that GMO foods fall into this category of "most cases in which we deliberately alter a gene"? What if in the case of GMO foods, we typically change a whole bunch of genes?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer helping us to argue "slight changes can still have big effects", an answer suggesting that "GMO foods are an typical case of deliberately altering the genetic structure of a plant, in that many genes are changed", or just an answer that helps us argue that "the health risks of GMO are significant".

old_notes.body: Whether genetically engineered plants have advantages over natural ones is irrelevant to the health risk question. The argument is about whether modified foods pose health risks, not about whether they offer benefits. Even if the modifications provide no advantages, that does not make them risky. And even if they provide enormous advantages, that does not make them safe. Benefits and risks are independent considerations. This answer addresses the value proposition of genetic engineering, not its safety profile. To weaken the scientist's argument about minimal risk, we need evidence that the modification COULD cause harm, not evidence about whether it provides benefits.

Saying that health risks may be "somewhat reduced by cooking" does not weaken the claim that the risks are minimal. If anything, it concedes that risks exist (they can be reduced) while offering a partial mitigation. But the scientist's argument is that the risks are minimal in the first place because the genetic change is so small. This answer does not address whether that reasoning is sound — it just offers a separate consideration about cooking that, if anything, suggests the risks are manageable rather than challenging whether they exist. To weaken the argument, we need evidence that small genetic changes CAN produce significant effects.

The fact that scientists have not yet identified which genes control each characteristic does not weaken the argument. If anything, it introduces uncertainty that could cut either way — maybe the changed genes are important, maybe they are not. Uncertainty about which genes control what does not establish that a single-gene change CAN produce significant harmful effects. To weaken the argument, we need affirmative evidence that small genetic changes can have outsized impacts, not merely an admission that we do not fully understand the genome. General scientific uncertainty does not specifically challenge the proportionality assumption.

This answer directly demolishes the scientist's proportionality assumption. The scientist argues that changing one gene in 750,000 is so slight it cannot have significant effects. This answer provides a concrete counterexample: some plants are known to be toxic, and their toxicity is known to result from a single gene. This proves that one gene — exactly the proportion of change the scientist dismisses as insignificant — can control a critically important trait like toxicity. If a single gene can make a plant toxic, then changing a single gene in a food plant could potentially make it toxic as well. The scientist's reasoning that "the change is too small to matter" collapses in the face of evidence that single genes can control consequential biological functions. The proportion of genetic material changed is irrelevant; what matters is the function of the specific gene that was altered.

What consumers opposed to genetic engineering know about genetic science has no bearing on whether the scientist's argument is logically sound. The scientist's claim is about the actual risk level of genetically modified food, not about what opponents know or do not know. Even if every opponent were scientifically illiterate, the argument could still be flawed. And even if every opponent were a geneticist, the argument could still be sound. The knowledge level of the opposition is irrelevant to whether the proportionality reasoning holds. This is an ad hominem consideration — attacking the credentials of those who disagree rather than engaging with the substantive question of risk.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: All animals can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Domesticated animals have come into existence by breeding only the tamest individuals of a wild species. If you breed only the individuals that show tameness when young, then after a number of generations you end up with a domesticated version of the animal, as with wolves becoming dogs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion is huge: "all animals" can be bred for domesticity. The evidence is one method and one example, wolves. The method needs a starting point: individuals that show tameness when young.

So how could we argue that not all animals can be bred for domesticity? Find a species where the method can't start. Say we try it with hyenas, and no hyena pup in any litter ever shows tameness. There's nothing to select, so there's no way to keep breeding tame with tame.

Notice "in principle." The conclusion isn't saying domestication is easy or fast. A slow, difficult breeding program still counts. To weaken, we need the method to be impossible for some species, not just harder.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying some species have no members that ever display tameness, or anything else that makes the breeding method impossible, not merely slower, for at least one kind of animal.

notes.body: A is about the reverse trip: turning domesticated animals back into wild ones. The conclusion is only about breeding toward domesticity. Whether the trip back works says nothing about whether every species can make the trip forward.

B says wild members mate more often than tame ones in some species. That slows the program, but a breeder chooses which animals breed, so the tame ones can still be paired. The conclusion only claims domestication is possible "in principle," and B doesn't make it impossible.

The method only works if some individuals "display tameness when young." C removes that starting point for some species: "no members ever display tameness." No tame animals means nothing to select and nothing to breed, so those species can't be domesticated this way, and "all animals" fails.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion says all, one counterexample weakens it. Find what the method requires, then look for a case where the requirement is missing.

D is the tempting one, since tame members being "less fertile" sounds like a real obstacle. But less fertile still means fertile. The tame animals still have offspring, so the program just takes longer, and the conclusion only says domestication is possible "in principle." D would work only if tame members couldn't reproduce at all.

E is about species already domesticated: some members are tamer than others. That is variation after the process has succeeded. It tells us nothing about a wild species that has no tame members to start with.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
old_steps.body: All animal can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Domesticated animals have come into existence by breeding only the tamest individuals of a wild species. If you only breed the individuals that show they're tame when they're young, then through successive generations of breeding you will "evolved" a domesticated version of the animal.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: How could the Defense make the case that "Nuh-uh ... not all animals can be bred for domesticity"? They could maybe say that for some species, none of the individuals are tame enough for us to start the selective breeding process. Maybe we're trying to domesticate a hyena, and we go through a litter of hyena babies, but none of them display tameness when young. If they we can't get our hands on multiple tame individuals, then we can't keep breeding tame-with-tame to get ever more tame versions of a hyena.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer saying "you can't always find some individuals that display tameness when young") or something that helps us argue that the conclusion is too universal, that some animals would not theoretically be eligible for the domestication process.

old_notes.body: The argument claims that wild animals can be domesticated through selective breeding. Whether domesticated animals can be turned back into wild ones through the reverse process is a completely separate question. The argument is about the feasibility of one-directional transformation — wild to domestic — and the reversibility of that process has no bearing on whether the forward process works for all species. Even if domesticated animals cannot be turned wild again, that tells us nothing about whether all wild species have the tame members needed to begin the domestication process. This answer addresses the reverse direction of a process when the argument is only about the forward direction.

The frequency of mating between wild and tame members does not address the argument's core assumption. The argument claims all animals can be domesticated by selectively breeding tame individuals. For this to fail, there must be species where the process cannot get started — where no tame individuals exist. Whether wild members mate more frequently than tame ones is a practical complication about breeding logistics, not a fundamental barrier to the process. As long as some tame individuals exist, a determined breeder could isolate them for selective breeding regardless of the mating preferences of wild members. The process might be slower or more difficult, but it would not be impossible in principle, and the argument's claim is about what is possible "in principle."

The argument's domestication process requires a specific starting condition: some members of the species must display tameness, so that a breeder can select and breed them. The argument then generalizes: since this process works (as demonstrated with wolves), all animals can be domesticated. But this generalization assumes that every species has at least some tame individuals to work with. This answer directly attacks that assumption by stating that in some animal species, no members ever display tameness. If there are zero tame individuals, the selective breeding process cannot begin — there is nothing to select for. The method is useless without the raw material it requires. This eliminates the precondition for domestication in at least some species, directly contradicting the universal claim that "all animals" can be bred for domesticity.

Lower fertility among tame members creates a practical challenge for selective breeding but does not make the process impossible in principle. The argument claims all animals can be domesticated "in principle," which concerns theoretical possibility rather than practical ease. Even if tame members are less fertile, they are not infertile — they can still reproduce, just at lower rates. A selective breeding program would take longer and be more difficult, but it could still proceed as long as tame individuals exist and can produce offspring. The argument's real vulnerability is the assumption that tame individuals exist in every species, not that the existing tame individuals breed at optimal rates. This answer identifies a speed bump, not a roadblock.

The existence of varying tameness levels within already-domesticated species tells us nothing about whether all wild species can be domesticated in the first place. The argument's claim is about the universality of the domestication process across species, not about variation within species that have already been domesticated. The fact that some dogs are tamer than others does not address whether, say, a completely wild species with no tame members can be domesticated. This answer describes a characteristic of the outcome of successful domestication rather than addressing whether the process can succeed universally. It is about post-domestication variation, while the argument's vulnerability concerns pre-domestication preconditions.

steps.label: Conclusion (So / clearly)
steps.body: Dr. Faris is in violation of the ethics code. Put another way: Dr. Faris deceived a patient about their medical treatment.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The ethics code says hospital staff must not deceive patients about their medical treatment. Dr. Faris gave medication A to a patient and said it would help the patient sleep, even though medication A has no known sleep-inducing properties. (The patient's sleep did improve after taking it.)

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion says Dr. Faris is "clearly" in violation. That depends on one thing: was the patient deceived? The only evidence of deception is that medication A has "no known sleep-inducing properties."

Given that, how could we argue Dr. Faris was honest in saying the medication would help the patient sleep? Look at the gap. A drug with no sleep-inducing properties can still help someone sleep by another route. Maybe it treats something that keeps the patient awake, like pain. The author even concedes that the patient's sleep did improve. If medication A helped through some indirect route, the statement was true, and a true statement isn't deception.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that gives medication A a real, indirect way to improve sleep, so that telling the patient it would help them sleep was true. That knocks out the deception, and the violation goes with it.

notes.body: A says Dr. Faris knew medication A had no known sleep-inducing properties. That makes the statement look more like knowing deception, not less. It strengthens the ethicist's case.
B says a committee is considering revisions to the code. The argument is about the code as it stands now. A possible future revision can't change whether Dr. Faris broke the current rule.

The ethicist treats "no known sleep-inducing properties" as if it meant the drug couldn't help anyone sleep. C pulls those apart: medication A "is a pain reliever that can indirectly lead to sleep" by easing discomfort. So telling the patient it would help them sleep was true, and a true statement isn't deception. No deception, no violation.

The move to repeat: when an argument calls a statement deceptive or false, look for a way the statement could be true after all.

D says other staff gave medication A to patients with trouble sleeping. Many people doing something doesn't make it honest. If the drug can't help with sleep, D only means more staff broke the code; it never gives a way the drug actually helps.

E rules out other medications as the reason the patient slept better. It's tempting, because it seems to point back to medication A. But sleep can improve for many reasons besides medication, and E gives no way medication A could help. C supplies that mechanism; E doesn't.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (So / clearly)
old_steps.body: Dr. Faris is in violation of the ethics code. rephrase: Dr. Faris deceived a patient about their medical treatment.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The ethic code says, "you mustn't deceive patients about their medical treatment". Dr. Faris gave medication A to a patient and told him it would help him sleep, even though it has no known sleep-inducing properties (although the patient's sleep did improve after taking medication A).

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: Is it clear that Dr. Faris deceived her patient? Is there any way that we could argue that even though Med A has no known sleep-inducing properties, she was still being honest in saying "this medication will help you sleep"? Maybe she thought the placebo effect would help the patient sleep. She knew the medication didn't have sleep altering properties, but she surmised that this patient probably would get some psychological comfort out of receiving some treatment, and that psychological comfort would lead to better sleep. Or maybe the Dr. was thinking that Med A would alleviate some condition that is keeping the patient awake at night. Maybe medication A does nothing for sleep, but it's good at alleviating the pain from headaches, and the patient can sleep when he has a headache. In that sense, she wouldn't have been deceptive to say "taking this med should help you sleep".

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer that gives us a way to argue that the Dr. genuinely believed that if the patient took this Med A, the process of doing so would help him sleep.

old_notes.body: If Dr. Faris was aware that medication A had no known sleep-inducing properties, this actually strengthens the case for an ethics violation. The argument concludes that Dr. Faris deceived the patient by telling him the medication would help him sleep when it has no such properties. If Dr. Faris knew this, the deception was intentional rather than the result of an honest mistake. Intentional deception is a stronger ethics violation than accidental misinformation. This answer makes the ethicist's case more compelling, not less, by establishing that the doctor knowingly told the patient something he had reason to believe was false.

Whether a committee is considering revisions to the ethics code has no bearing on whether Dr. Faris violated the current code. The ethicist's argument is about whether the doctor's conduct violated the existing rules, not about whether those rules might change in the future. Even if the ethics code is revised tomorrow, that does not retroactively alter whether Dr. Faris's statement constituted deception under the code as it currently stands. Future changes to the rules cannot excuse past violations of them. This answer introduces information about potential future policy that is completely irrelevant to the backward-looking question of whether a violation occurred.

This answer provides the indirect mechanism that makes Dr. Faris's statement truthful. If medication A is a pain reliever that reduces pain, and that pain reduction indirectly leads to better sleep, then telling the patient the medication would help him sleep was accurate — not deceptive. The medication genuinely helps the patient sleep, just not through direct sleep-inducing properties. The ethicist's reasoning assumed that "no known sleep-inducing properties" means "cannot help with sleep," but this answer shows that assumption is wrong. A medication can legitimately improve sleep by addressing an underlying condition — in this case, pain — that was preventing sleep. Since Dr. Faris's statement turns out to be truthful, there was no deception, and therefore no violation of the ethics code. The entire argument unravels because the central premise — that Dr. Faris deceived the patient — is shown to be false.

Other staff members prescribing medication A for sleep difficulties tells us that Dr. Faris was not alone in the practice, but it does not establish whether the practice was actually deceptive. Widespread behavior does not determine whether that behavior is truthful or deceptive. If medication A truly cannot help with sleep, then many doctors are violating the ethics code — the violation is just more widespread. If medication A can help with sleep, then we need to know why, which this answer does not explain. The fact that others did the same thing is relevant to whether Dr. Faris should be singled out, but not to whether the statement itself was deceptive. The ethicist's argument is about the nature of the act, not about how many people committed it.

If Dr. Faris knew the patient was not taking any other sleep-inducing medications, this eliminates the possibility that the patient's improved sleep was caused by something other than medication A. But the ethicist's argument is not about whether the patient's sleep actually improved — the ethicist acknowledges it did. The argument is about whether Dr. Faris's statement was deceptive at the time it was made, given that medication A has no known sleep-inducing properties. Knowing that no other medications contributed to the sleep improvement, if anything, makes the situation more puzzling but does not provide a legitimate basis for Dr. Faris's claim. It does not establish a mechanism by which medication A helps sleep, so it does not show the statement was truthful.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: The government should require drug companies to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Relatively minor drug-related interactions can still be harmful to patients (such as the fact that fruit juice can render aspirin ineffective, leading to people either not getting the pain relief they expected or to people taking more aspirin than necessary).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a recommendation, so ask what could go wrong with the plan. Given that relatively minor interactions can still hurt patients, as with aspirin and fruit juice, how could we argue the government should not require notice of "all known drug-related interactions"?

The author shows one upside. Look for downsides. Would it cost too much? Is it even possible? Could it backfire? Picture a drug insert listing forty interactions, most as mild as the fruit juice one. Would a patient still notice the one that could put them in the hospital? A plan meant to protect patients could end up hiding the warnings that matter most.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a downside of requiring notice of every known interaction: it costs too much, it can't be done, or it backfires, for example by burying serious warnings under minor ones.

notes.body:
A shows the plan backfires. The advocate wants every interaction listed to protect patients. But listing minor ones "would detract from a patient’s attention to serious interactions." The plan meant to protect patients would leave them less protected from the interactions that matter most.

The move to repeat: on a recommendation, a strong weakener is a cost that undercuts the plan's own goal.

B says many drugs have fewer documented interactions than aspirin. That means shorter lists for those drugs, but the requirement still applies to them. Fewer interactions makes notice easier, if anything, so B gives no reason to drop the plan.

C says notice of every interaction would cause "only negligible price increases for consumers." Cost was a possible objection to the plan, and C takes it away. That helps the advocate. A weakener needs a real downside, not the removal of one.
D says many interactions haven't been identified yet. The plan only covers "all known" interactions, so the unknown ones are outside it. D shows no harm from listing the known ones.
E says pharmacists usually point patients to printed warnings. That suggests warnings actually get read, which makes notice look more useful. It strengthens the case for the plan.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
old_steps.body: The government should require drug companies to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Relatively minor drug-related interactions can still be harmful to patients (such as the fact that fruit juice can render aspirin ineffective, leading to people either not getting the pain relief they expected or to people taking more aspirin than necessary).

old_steps.body: Given that ... relatively minor drug-related interactions can be harmful to patients (such as the fruit juice / aspirin example), How can we argue that ... drug companies should not be required to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions? The author is presenting one potential upside of this Plan / Recommendation (people taking aspirin would realize not to take it with fruit juice). We should try to think of potential downsides.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer bringing up something negative about the plan of requiring drug companies to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions. Is there some way in which it wouldn't be feasible or cost prohibitive? (Maybe it's impossible or impossibly costly to figure out every single way a new drug could interact with every other substance. Could it backfire in some way? (would people suddenly be afraid to take their needed medicines because they read about a possible interaction that is extremely rare but scares them out of taking their meds?)

old_notes.body: This answer identifies the self-defeating consequence of the proposed policy. The consumer advocate wants all drug interactions disclosed so patients can avoid harmful interactions. But if the volume of information about minor interactions overwhelms patients, they will pay less attention to the serious, potentially life-threatening interactions that matter most. The policy would achieve the opposite of its intended purpose: instead of making patients safer, it would make them less safe by diluting their attention across a massive list of interactions, most of which are minor. The aspirin-and-fruit-juice type interactions would crowd out warnings about interactions that could cause organ damage, severe allergic reactions, or death. This is a classic "more is not always better" weakener — the proposed remedy creates a new problem that is worse than the original one.

The fact that many drugs have fewer interactions than aspirin does not undermine the consumer advocate's argument. The advocate's proposal covers all drugs, not just aspirin. Even if most drugs have fewer interactions, the policy still requires disclosure of all known interactions for every drug. A drug with five interactions instead of fifty still requires those five to be disclosed under the proposed policy. The volume of information per drug is not the issue — the advocate's argument is about the principle of comprehensive disclosure regardless of quantity. This answer provides context about the aspirin example but does not challenge the reasoning or the policy recommendation in any meaningful way.

If providing information about all interactions would result in only negligible price increases for consumers, this removes a potential practical objection to the policy, but it does not address the argument's logical vulnerability. The consumer advocate's argument could be weakened by showing the policy would be ineffective or counterproductive, not by showing it would be inexpensive. The cost of implementation is a practical concern, and showing that costs are negligible actually makes the policy look more feasible, not less desirable. This answer addresses a potential objection (cost) that the argument never raised, and it addresses it in a way that supports the policy rather than undermining it. The real weakness is about information overload, not financial burden.

The fact that many interactions have not yet been identified is irrelevant to whether the government should require disclosure of those that have been identified. The advocate's proposal covers "all known" interactions, and the existence of unknown ones does not affect the case for disclosing known ones. If anything, this answer might slightly strengthen the advocate's position by suggesting the problem is even larger than currently understood — but that would only affect the scope of future disclosure, not the current proposal. The argument is about whether known interactions should be disclosed, not about the completeness of current research.

If pharmacists draw patients' attention to printed warnings, this supports the idea that disclosure actually works — people do read and act on the information they receive. The consumer advocate argues that patients should be given interaction information, and this answer confirms that when warnings are provided, healthcare professionals help ensure patients notice them. Rather than weakening the argument, this answer provides evidence that the disclosure mechanism is effective: warnings are not ignored but are actively communicated by pharmacists. This makes the case for comprehensive disclosure stronger, since it suggests the information would actually reach and influence patients.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The government's tax collection agency has not followed through on its plan to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Audits are the primary tool for detecting corporate income tax violations, and over the past year since they announced the plan, not a single audit of corporate income tax returns has been completed.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author's case: audits are the primary way to detect violations, no corporate audit has been completed in a year, so the agency hasn't followed through on its crackdown.

Given that not a single corporate audit was completed in the past year, how could we still argue the agency is following through? Look at the word "completed." The author assumes a real crackdown would produce finished audits within a year. What if audits take longer than that? Then the agency could have started hundreds of audits the day after the announcement, and the count of completed audits would still be zero.

Another route: the agency may be cracking down by other means. Audits are the "primary" tool, not the only one.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that gives an innocent reason for zero completed audits, most likely that audits take more than a year to finish. Or an answer showing the agency is cracking down some other way.

notes.body: A says the crackdown is part of a broad campaign against corporate misconduct. That describes the plan's scope, not whether anything is being done. A broad campaign can still be doing nothing, and zero completed audits is just as unexplained.

B is about personal income tax audits; the crackdown is about corporate income tax law. More personal audits shows the agency is busy, but not with this plan. If anything, it makes the lack of corporate audits look like a choice.

C says most corporate audits don't turn up significant violations. That might make audits seem less worth doing, but it neither explains why none were completed nor shows any crackdown effort. The evidence of zero completed audits stands.

The argument assumes a real crackdown would show completed audits within a year. D says it "generally takes longer than one year to complete an audit." Now zero completed audits is exactly what we'd expect even if the agency began auditing the day it announced the plan. The evidence no longer points to inaction.

The move to repeat: when evidence counts results over a period, ask whether results could even arrive in that time.

E compares the last five years with the five before: fewer audits completed. That is a longer trend of doing less, which fits the idea that the agency isn't serious. It doesn't explain the past year's zero, so it can't weaken.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: The government's tax collection agency has not followed through on its plan to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law.

old_steps.body: Audits are the primary tool for detecting corporate income tax violations, and over the past year since they announced the plan, not a single audit of corporate income tax returns has been completed.

old_steps.body:
Given that .... there hasn't been a single audit completed since the govt tax agency pledged to crack down on violations of corp tax law.
How could we still argue that ... the govt tax agency has followed through on its plan to crack down on violations of corp income tax law?
Maybe they're trying to crack down through methods that don't involve audits? We know that audits are the primary tool for detecting such violations, but maybe the govt. is focusing on some of the less-used methods. Maybe they don't need to detect violations (they're already aware of them); they just need the will and manpower to go confront these corporations and charge them with violations.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Let's look for an answer that allows us to "make an excuse" for the fact that not a single audit has been completed, or allows us to argue that the government really is dedicated to cracking down on violations of corp income tax law.

old_notes.body: Knowing that the corporate audits are part of a broader campaign against corporate misconduct does not explain why none of them have been completed. The argument's concern is specifically about the lack of completed audits, and expanding the scope of the initiative does not address the timeline issue. A broader campaign might involve more audits or different types of enforcement, but that has no bearing on whether any individual corporate audit has been finished. The question remains: if the crackdown is genuine, why has nothing been completed in a year? This answer leaves that question entirely unanswered.

The argument is entirely about corporate tax audits. What the agency does with personal income tax returns is a separate enforcement activity that has no bearing on whether the corporate crackdown is genuine. Even if the agency has dramatically increased its personal income tax auditing, that says nothing about why corporate audits remain incomplete. These are different types of audits targeting different populations with different procedures and timelines. Introducing personal tax audit data shifts attention to an irrelevant metric rather than addressing the specific gap the argument identifies: zero completed corporate audits after a year of a supposedly genuine corporate crackdown.

If most completed audits do not reveal significant violations, this actually makes the agency's failure to complete any audits look worse, not better. The argument concludes the crackdown is not genuine because nothing has been completed. To weaken that conclusion, we need a reason why the absence of completed audits is consistent with genuine effort. This answer does not provide one. Instead, it suggests that even when audits are completed, they tend to come up empty — which, if anything, bolsters the skeptic's case by adding a second layer of futility. Not only has nothing been finished, but even finished audits are typically unproductive. This pushes in the wrong direction entirely.

The argument's logic depends on a hidden assumption: a genuine crackdown would produce completed audits within one year. This answer directly attacks that assumption by establishing that corporate audits inherently take longer than a year to complete. If the audit process itself requires more than twelve months, then the absence of completed audits is not evidence of inaction — it is simply evidence that the work is still in progress. The agency could have initiated dozens of thorough audits on the day of the announcement, and every single one of them would still be incomplete after twelve months. This provides an innocent, alternative explanation for the apparently damning evidence: the audits exist and are underway, but the process has not yet run its course. By showing that the timeline expectation is unreasonable, this answer severs the connection between "no results yet" and "no genuine effort."

A five-year decline in completed audits reveals a longer-term pattern of weakening enforcement, which actually supports the skeptic's conclusion rather than undermining it. The argument claims the crackdown is not genuine, and a multi-year trend of declining audit activity makes that claim more plausible, not less. If the agency has been pulling back from enforcement for half a decade, the current zero-completion figure looks like the continuation of a broader retreat rather than an isolated anomaly. A weakening answer needs to make the crackdown look genuine despite the lack of results. This answer makes it look like part of a sustained pattern of doing less — the opposite of what is needed.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Whenever lawyers engage in obstructive behaviors (such as inflammatory language or badgering witnesses), it's reasonable to doubt whether the eventual verdict is correct.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: These obstructive behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument slides between two ideas.

Idea one: obstructive behavior hinders the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.
Idea two: obstructive behavior makes it reasonable to doubt that a correct verdict was reached.

A strong headwind might hinder my effort to reach the top of Mt. Whitney. But if I'm standing at the summit, the headwind gives you no reason to doubt I got there.

Same here. Obstructive behavior can make the jury's job harder without making a wrong verdict likely. Given that these behaviors hinder the jury, how could we argue the verdict still deserves trust? Show that juries usually get past the obstruction anyway. And notice "Whenever": the conclusion covers every trial with such behavior, so anything showing the behavior rarely changes outcomes hurts it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying these behaviors rarely change what the jury decides, so even when lawyers use them, the verdict is probably still correct.

notes.body: A says strict judges sometimes preside over incorrect verdicts. The conclusion is about trials with obstructive behavior, and A is about trials without it. Wrong verdicts happening elsewhere doesn't show that badgering witnesses is harmless.

B says lawyers care less than judges about whether outcomes are just. That is about motives. The question is whether the tactics actually distort verdicts, and lawyers who care little about justice are, if anything, more likely to try.

C says people swayed by inflammatory language rarely admit it later. That makes the influence harder to detect, which gives us more reason to doubt verdicts, not less. It pushes toward the conclusion.

The conclusion needs obstructive behavior to actually threaten the verdict. D says it "is seldom effective in cases where jurors are also presented with legitimate evidence." In a typical trial jurors do hear legitimate evidence, so the badgering usually changes nothing, and the mere fact that it happened is weak grounds for doubting the verdict.

The move to repeat: when an argument goes from a hindrance to a doubtful result, look for an answer showing the job still gets done.
E says jurors are screened partly for bias. That happens before trial. A juror who starts out unbiased can still be swayed by badgering during it, so E doesn't show the behavior is harmless.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Whenever lawyers engage in obstructive behaviors (such as inflammatory language or badgering witnesses), it's reasonable to doubt whether the eventual verdict is correct.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: These obstructive behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
They seem to be testing the tension between these two concepts:
"Thing X hinders the effort to reach a correct verdict"
vs.
"Thing X causes us to doubt that a correct verdict was reached".
A strong headwind might hinder my effort to reach the top of Mt. Whitney, but a strong headwind doesn't make it reasonable to doubt my claim that I reached the top of Mt. Whitney.
In other words, yes, these obstructive behaviors make it harder to reach a verdict, but that's different from saying they make it somewhat likely that I'll reach the wrong verdict.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer saying, "These behaviors might make it harder to reach a verdict, but they don't undermine our trust that if the jury managed to reach a verdict, it was a correct one."

old_notes.body: This answer shifts focus from lawyer behavior to judge behavior. The argument claims that inflammatory LAWYER tactics give reason to doubt verdicts. Whether strict JUDGES sometimes preside over wrong verdicts is a different question entirely. Information about judges and their verdicts provides no evidence about the specific effect of lawyer misconduct on verdict accuracy. To weaken the argument, we need evidence specifically about the relationship between inflammatory lawyer tactics and verdict outcomes — not about what happens under a different courtroom variable.

Whether lawyers care more about winning than about justice addresses their motivations, not the effectiveness of their tactics. The argument's conclusion is about whether inflammatory behavior actually compromises verdicts. A lawyer could be entirely motivated by winning and still fail to distort the verdict with inflammatory tactics, or a justice-seeking lawyer could accidentally distort proceedings. Motivation and effectiveness are independent variables. The weakener must show that inflammatory language does not actually lead to incorrect verdicts — not that lawyers have bad intentions.

If people influenced by inflammatory language are unlikely to admit it, the distorting effect could be even more widespread and harder to detect than assumed. Jurors might be swayed by emotional manipulation without recognizing or acknowledging it, making compromised verdicts invisible. This makes the argument's concern MORE warranted, not less — the influence is insidious and undetectable. A weakener should give us reason to trust verdicts despite the presence of inflammatory tactics. This answer does the opposite by suggesting the problem is worse than it appears.

This answer directly breaks the link between inflammatory behavior and incorrect verdicts. The argument assumes that when lawyers use inflammatory tactics, the verdict is likely compromised. But if obstructive behavior "seldom" succeeds when jurors are also presented with legitimate evidence, then the evidence — not the theatrics — determines the outcome in the vast majority of cases.

In real trials, legitimate evidence is almost always presented. If inflammatory behavior is ineffective against actual evidence, then its presence gives little reason to doubt the verdict. The tactics might be unprofessional and obnoxious, but they do not accomplish what the argument fears: distorting the jury's decision. This directly undermines the conclusion that we should doubt verdicts whenever inflammatory behavior occurs, because the behavior simply does not have the distorting effect the argument claims it does.

Jury selection procedures occur before the trial. The argument is about what happens during the trial when lawyers engage in inflammatory behavior. These are different stages of the legal process. Even if jury selection perfectly screens out all pre-existing biases, the selected jurors could still be influenced by inflammatory tactics that occur during the proceedings themselves. Pre-trial screening cannot immunize jurors against in-trial manipulation. The argument's concern is about in-trial influence, and this answer addresses pre-trial preparation — a different phase entirely.
